Slime
SLYME
noun
From the Old English slīm, “slime, mire”; in the KJV it renders the Hebrew word for bitumen or asphalt — the natural pitch that seeps out of the ground in Mesopotamia and about the Salt Sea, used anciently as mortar and as waterproofing.

Biblical Definition

Slime in the Authorized Version is not pond scum but bitumen — the black asphalt that oozes from the earth in Mesopotamia and about the vale of Siddim, used by the ancients for mortar and for caulking. It appears at the two ends of a great contrast. At Babel the builders said “one to another, Go to, let us make brick, and burn them throughly. And they had brick for stone, and slime had they for morter” (Gen 11:3), and with that brick and slime they undertook a tower “whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name” (Gen 11:4). Here is man’s religion in one verse: a manufactured stone, a manufactured mortar, a self-made stair to God, and a name of his own getting. The LORD came down, confounded the tongue, and called the place Babel (Gen 11:9). But the same slime appears again in gentler hands: when Moses’ mother could hide him no longer, “she took for him an ark of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime and with pitch, and put the child therein” (Exo 2:3), and the pitch of the earth kept the water out and the deliverer alive. The identical substance builds the tower of rebellion and seals the ark of salvation. What men gather to make themselves a name, God takes up to save His people; and the difference is never in the tar but in whose hand is spreading it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Bitumen or asphalt; the natural pitch of the ground, used anciently for mortar and for waterproofing — the morter of Babel and the daubing of Moses’ ark.

SLIME, a soft, viscous earth; in Scripture, bitumen or asphalt.

From the Saxon slīm, “slime, mire”; not pond scum but the pitch of the ground.

It seeps naturally from the earth in Shinar and about the vale of Siddim.

At Babel they had brick for stone, and slime had they for morter (Gen 11:3).

With slime and pitch the ark of bulrushes was daubed for Moses (Exo 2:3).

Key Scripture

Gen 11:3 — "And they said one to another, Go to, let us make brick, and burn them throughly. And they had brick for stone, and slime had they for morter."

Gen 11:4 — "And they said, Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth."

Gen 11:9 — "Therefore is the name of it called Babel; because the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth: and from thence did the LORD scatter them abroad upon the face of all the earth."

Exo 2:3 — "And when she could not longer hide him, she took for him an ark of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime and with pitch, and put the child therein; and she laid it in the flags by the river's brink."

Modern Corruption

The live corruption is the reading of Babel as a charming tale that explains why men speak different tongues — instead of a real rebellion really judged, and man’s brick-and-slime project still going up.

expand to see more

There is a live corruption here, and it comes wearing academic clothes: Babel read as a pleasant tale invented after the fact to explain why men speak different tongues — a story about language rather than a rebellion against God. Moses is not writing a fable. He names the plain of Shinar, the building material, the mortar, the purpose, and the LORD’s own descent and judgment; and Genesis hangs the whole table of the nations on it. The details are the details of a builder: brick because Shinar has no stone, slime because Shinar has bitumen. To dissolve that into a story is to take from the church a real judgment on a real sin, and to leave in its place a curiosity. Archaeology may confirm the brick and the bitumen of the Mesopotamian ziggurats; it does not sit in judgment on the Word that told us about them. The canonical narrative is the authority, and the spade is the corroborating witness.

The deeper corruption is the project itself, and it has never stopped. Brick for stone and slime for morter: a manufactured substitute for what God gives, mortared with what men scrape off the ground, raised to reach heaven and to make us a name. That is the religion of the natural heart in one sentence — a stair built upward by human hands, so that we may arrive at God on our terms and be famous for it. And the LORD came down. He always must; the tower never reaches. Yet mark the mercy hidden in the same black pitch: the slime that mortared Babel also daubed the little ark of bulrushes that carried Moses over the water of a king’s decree. God takes the very stuff of man’s self-salvation and uses it to save His own. We do not climb to Him; He comes down — at Babel to scatter, at Bethlehem to redeem.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means bitumen or asphalt, the natural pitch of the ground used as mortar.

expand to see more

Slime — Old English slīm, “slime, mire.”

In Scripture it renders the Hebrew for bitumen or asphalt, not pond scum.

It seeps from the ground in Shinar and about the vale of Siddim.

At Babel it was the morter of man’s self-made tower (Gen 11:3).

It also daubed the ark of bulrushes that preserved Moses (Exo 2:3).

Usage

"They had brick for stone, and slime had they for morter — man’s own stair to heaven."

"Let us make us a name: Babel’s slime is the mortar of every self-salvation project."

"The same slime daubed the ark of bulrushes: God uses the pitch of the earth to save."
